The wind screamed against the reinforced glass of the lantern room, a high-pitched shriek that vibrated through Elias’s teeth. Rain lashed the tower in horizontal sheets, turning the world outside into a churning gray void. Inside, the air smelled of ozone, kerosene, and the damp rot of old wood. Elias wiped his brow with a sleeve stained by decades of salt and soot. He was checking the lens mechanism, a routine he had performed every night for thirty years, when his hand brushed against something wedged behind the brass housing.

It was a cylinder of oilskin, brittle and cracked. Curiosity, a dangerous habit for a man who lived by routine, compelled him to unroll it. The paper was yellowed, the ink faded to a bruised purple. It was a map, but not of any chart he knew. The coastlines were distorted, exaggerated, as if drawn by someone who had seen the sea not as a boundary, but as a living, breathing entity. A red circle marked a spot near the reef, labeled in a shaky hand: *Here, the tide forgets.*
